slides.text: Shortest stretch of [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3] with sum ≥ 7? Trying every start and every end is O(n²).
slides.alt: "Shortest stretch with sum ≥ 7?" over the array 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, with "every start × every end = O(n²)".

slides.text: the front stretches forward to grab new ground, and when it's overreached, the back pulls in. Neither end ever backs up.
slides.alt: The same array with the rule "front stretches forward →, back pulls in →, neither end ever backs up".
A window around 1, 2, 4 at indices 2 to 4: window total = 7 ≥ 7 ✓, shortest so far = 3.
The window now around 4, 3 at indices 4 and 5: window total = 7 ≥ 7 ✓, shortest so far = 2, and the tag "answer: [4, 3], length 2".

slides.text: Both pointers only move forward, so it's O(n) even with a loop inside a loop.
slides.alt: Python min_subarray_len(target, nums) with the shrink step, total -= nums[left], highlighted inside while total >= target. The note reads "drop nums[left], move left on"; the stage shows the window on 2, 4 with left and right pointers: record 3, drop 1 → total 6.

slides.text: Our test run on 10,000 numbers (Python): 848 ms checking every stretch vs 1.18 ms for the window.
slides.alt: "10,000 numbers, our test run, Python": every start × every end takes 848 ms; the sliding window takes 1.18 ms.

slides.text: The trap: write if instead of while and the window shrinks at most once per step.
slides.alt: "The trap: if instead of while": while total >= target: gives 2 ✓; if total >= target: gives 4 ✗. It shrinks at most once per step, so the window never gets tight.
